steps.message:
You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    },
    {
      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

Task Description:
Warehouse snapshot desk exposes /app/bin/dewkiln (native ELF, first bytes \x7fELF). Drive clasp so it loads /app/daywell, emits /app/bloturn/ledger.json and /app/bloturn/check.json, packs /app/packbay/stage, and lays the same calendar names under /app/packbay/latest. /app/millrib/sheet.tpl fills check.json. Pipeline crates are named in /app/opstext/LIST.txt. Correct the pipeline modules under /app/environment. A script or interpreter is not enough. A hand-written ledger is not enough; static copies of check.json are insufficient. The verifier reruns /app/bin/dewkiln clasp.

clasp still returns 0 with a non-empty ledger, but /app/packbay/latest has none of the rows from the most recently populated calendar file even though /app/daywell still holds that file with rows in it. After clasp, that calendar file's restored row count must equal a count taken from /app/daywell without reading ledger.json. check.json schema fields are {probe, matched, taken}: probe is the string live; matched and taken are integers equal to the live daywell row total for calendar days at or before the wall. A run whose check never opened the /app/daywell files must return non-zero and must not write /app/bloturn/GUARD (false). Success writes GUARD containing ok. An empty /app/daywell must also return non-zero with GUARD absent (false). A calendar file whose day is past the wall integer must not appear under /app/packbay/latest (false). Calendar files use the dYYYYMMDD.tbl name with one row id per line. The wall calendar integer lives in /app/opstext/WALL. The CI floor integer lives in /app/floorcue/MIN.txt.

steps.message:
Analysis: There is no literal /app/environment directory; the pipeline crates are the listed source directories. Current clasp is demonstrably wrong: it reports 15 rows, uses probe "ledger", and latest omits d20260912 and d20260913. The live total through WALL=20260913 is 22 rows. Stage has d10–d12, while latest only d10–d11, suggesting separate defects across selection, packing, and restoration. We must inspect all Rust sources and build script, then patch and rebuild the native ELF.
Plan: Read every Rust source, the build script, notes, and shift configuration with line numbers. Inspect binary strings if useful to understand crate linkage. Based on those interfaces, patch the relevant modules so clasp reads live daywell files, counts all valid days through WALL, renders the template as probe live with matched=taken=22, stages and restores every eligible calendar file, excludes future dates, enforces the CI floor, and only writes GUARD on full success.

echo '===== wick.sh ====='; nl -ba /app/wick.sh; echo '===== NOTE ====='; cat /app/corkpit/NOTE.txt; echo '===== SHIFT ====='; cat /app/opstext/SHIFT.txt; echo '===== usage ====='; cat /app/wickmill/usage.txt; echo '===== rust toolchain ====='; rustc --version; cargo --version 2>/dev/null || true

steps.message:
Analysis: The defects visible so far are: rim excludes the wall day (`<` instead of `<=`), soak deliberately drops the newest selected file, gait hard-codes probe `ledger`, boot ignores the floor result, and empty input is treated as success. Counting is currently done from staged copies rather than directly establishing the live daywell total for check. We still need the complete read.rs and skip.rs bodies because skip may mutate staged files and read/list behavior controls valid filename handling. rustc is not on PATH despite the rebuild script, so we must locate a Rust compiler or use an available native compiler to produce the required ELF.
Plan: Inspect the omitted source files and locate compilers/toolchains. Then patch all defective modules and orchestrator semantics. Prefer rebuilding with Rust if rustc exists elsewhere; otherwise compile a native C implementation to /app/bin/dewkiln while also correcting the Rust module sources. The implementation will clean GUARD first, reject empty/no eligible daywell and below-floor totals, include days <= wall only, count rows by opening live daywell files, stage and restore identical eligible files, render the supplied template with live/total/total, and create GUARD only after every operation succeeds.

Filename parsing is too permissive, selection excludes the wall day, restoration drops the newest file, row-reading errors are silently converted to zero, empty input succeeds, the floor result is ignored, and check.json uses the wrong probe. A usable Rust compiler exists at /usr/local/rustup/toolchains/1.85.1-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bin/rustc, but wick.sh does not include it.
Plan: Rewrite the affected Rust modules with strict calendar-name recognition, inclusive wall filtering, fallible live-file row counting, complete restoration, proper failure behavior, floor enforcement, and dynamic template rendering with probe live. Update wick.sh to locate the installed compiler, rebuild the native ELF, and run baseline plus negative/inclusion tests while restoring fixtures afterward.
